assumptions.proposition: The patient has acute right upper quadrant abdominal pain with recurrent nausea and vomiting shortly after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with recent GJ stricture dilation, raising concern for a postoperative intra-abdominal complication.
evidence: “reports acute onset of RUQ abdominal pain which he denies having previously”
“S/P Roun En Y Gastric Bypass ___ with GJ stenosis dilated x 2 post op.”

assumptions.proposition: Prior plain abdominal radiography has not shown free air or clear obstruction, so more subtle or non-perforative complications (e.g., internal hernia, leak not causing free air, abscess, biliary pathology) remain possible.
assumptions.level: possible mechanisms of abdominal pain after surgery
evidence: “There is no evidence of free air.  Nonspecific bowel gas pattern is seen.”
“Post-surgical changes related to Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with suture material within the left abdomen are noted.”

assumptions.proposition: Gallbladder or biliary disease is a possible cause of new RUQ pain after rapid postoperative weight loss and gastric bypass.
assumptions.level: specific potential source of RUQ pain
evidence: “reports acute onset of RUQ abdominal pain which he denies having previously”
“Abd: obese, soft, with moderate TTP in RUQ, non-distended, no rebound/guarding.”

assumptions.proposition: Current laboratory studies show no leukocytosis, normal lactate, and only mildly elevated ALT, so there is not yet clear biochemical evidence of sepsis, bowel ischemia, or severe hepatobiliary obstruction.
evidence: “White Blood Cells: 8.3 K/uL (ref 4.0-11.0)”
“Lactate: 1.4 mmol/L (ref 0.5-2.0)”

assumptions.proposition: The prior GJ stricture, although recently dilated, may have recurred or there may be another mechanical problem affecting the gastric bypass limbs contributing to vomiting and pain.
assumptions.level: status and function of surgical anastomosis
evidence: “he underwent an EGD which revealed a G-J stricture, which was dilated at that time.”
“Upon taking POs he again began having nausea and reports vomiting 4 times”

current_question.primary: What is the structural cause of this patient’s new right upper quadrant abdominal pain and recurrent vomiting shortly after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and GJ dilation?
current_question.target: postoperative abdominal organs and Roux-en-Y anatomy (including bowel, anastomoses, mesentery, and hepatobiliary structures)
current_question.positive_answer_changes: Identifying a specific complication (e.g., leak, internal hernia, obstruction, abscess, or biliary pathology) would prompt targeted management such as surgical consultation, possible re-operation, drainage, or focused medical therapy.
current_question.negative_answer_changes: If no significant structural complication is identified, clinicians may favor non-surgical causes, adjust analgesia and antiemetics, consider endoscopic reassessment of the anastomosis, or further hepatobiliary workup (e.g., ultrasound, HIDA).
secondary_questions: Is there imaging evidence of a complication of the Roux-en-Y reconstruction such as anastomotic leak, obstruction, or internal hernia?
Is there any biliary or hepatic pathology that could explain the new right upper quadrant pain?

answer_requirements.dimension: Adequate contrast-enhanced visualization of the post-gastric-bypass anatomy, including gastric pouch, Roux limb, biliopancreatic limb, and surrounding mesentery, as well as liver and gallbladder.
answer_requirements.why_required: The structural source of the symptoms can only be determined if these postoperative structures and adjacent organs are well visualized.

answer_requirements.dimension: Presence or absence and character of specific postoperative complications such as anastomotic leak, localized fluid collection/abscess, internal hernia, bowel obstruction, or mesenteric ischemia.
answer_requirements.why_required: Determining whether there is a treatable surgical complication is central to guiding urgent management.

answer_requirements.dimension: Presence or absence of hepatobiliary abnormalities (e.g., gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, biliary dilation, focal hepatic lesions) that could explain RUQ pain.
answer_requirements.why_required: Biliary disease is a common and important alternative cause of new RUQ pain after bariatric surgery and needs to be assessed.

answer_requirements.dimension: Extent and severity of any identified complication (e.g., size of fluid collection, degree of obstruction, amount of bowel involved).
answer_requirements.why_required: Management decisions (operative vs conservative, urgency, and type of intervention) depend on how extensive and severe any complication is.

evidence: “reports acute onset of RUQ abdominal pain which he denies having previously”
“Upon taking POs he again began having nausea and reports vomiting 4 times”

supporting_evidence: “UPRIGHT AND SUPINE VIEWS OF THE ABDOMEN: There is no evidence of free air.  Nonspecific bowel gas pattern is seen.  Post-surgical changes related to Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with suture material within the left abdomen are noted.”
requirements.reason: Plain abdominal radiographs show gross postsurgical changes and exclude free air but cannot adequately visualize the detailed postoperative anatomy, mesentery, or solid organs needed to localize the structural source of symptoms.

supporting_evidence: “There is no evidence of free air.  Nonspecific bowel gas pattern is seen.”
requirements.reason: Absence of free air makes frank perforation less likely and there is no radiographic obstruction pattern, but plain films do not exclude internal hernia, contained leak, abscess, or subtle obstruction, so major complications are not ruled out.

supporting_evidence: “Abd: obese, soft, with moderate TTP in RUQ, non-distended, no rebound/guarding.”
requirements.reason: No imaging of the hepatobiliary system has been performed; labs show only a mildly elevated ALT with normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase, which neither confirms nor excludes biliary pathology.

supporting_evidence: “There is no evidence of free air.  Nonspecific bowel gas pattern is seen.”
requirements.reason: While lack of free air suggests no obvious catastrophic perforation, there is no imaging information on size or extent of any possible collections, obstruction, or ischemia, so severity cannot be determined.

coverage.aggregate_reason: Plain radiographs exclude free intraperitoneal air and gross obstruction but do not adequately visualize postoperative anatomy, detect subtle or contained complications, or assess hepatobiliary causes or severity, leaving the main question incompletely answered.

answer_requirements.why_required: The patient has recent surgery with prior G-J stricture; identifying or excluding new complications is central to explaining recurrent symptoms.
